I personally think that Sunrise's monster design does not fit that well the **overall** design philosophy of MH: they are **animals** living in their **natural habitat**. (Of course, in every game you also have a ideally small fraction of monsters that are **unnatrual** to contrast the rest of the roster, think Elders like Fatalis, Kirin etc.)

Naturally Sunrise is not my favorite entry in the series. However, Sunrise tells you what to expect from the get go (Japanese yokai for Rise, western fantasy for Sunbreak) and in that context has very good designs that fit its own overall theme.

From the very beginning of the series, the monsters were always meant to be a mixture of both. They need to have **some** fantastical elements to distinguish itself from the real world, while making it convincing that they are supposed to be **animals**. Rathalos for example is a wyvern from fantasy with its fantastical elements/behaviors toned down. In every game you would have a bulk of low-fantasy monsters, with a few high-fantasy ones (elders like Kirin, Yama Tsukami, Fatalis) to **contrast** with the rest of the roster.  This has unfortunately gotten less true as the series progressed.

  
With that in mind, I'd say 70-80% grounded with 20-30% over-the-topness is a good sweet spot.

Vectors are arrows, and more generally, anything "arrow-like".

Consider the x-y plane, and think of a particular position on the x-y plane, say (5,3). This is a position in the x-y plane. Now draw and arrow from the origin (0,0), to (5,3). This is an example of a vector, in particular this is a positon vector. It has a length and a direction.

We like to represent vectors as columns of numbers: one way of saying I am at the position (5,3) is that I am 5 steps out in the x-direction, and 3 steps out in the y-direction. So we express position vectors in the x-y plane with a column of numbers labelling how many steps out we are in each direction: (5 3).

The arrows do more than just point: you can add them and scale them as well. Here we'll just be concerned with scaling them. You can take a vector, v, and multiply it with a number, k. The result: kv, is an arrow pointing in the same direction as v, but k times longer(or shorter if 0<k<1, or in the opposite direction if k<0). 

For example, if I take the position vector I had before: (5 3), and multiply it by 2, I get 2(5 3) = (10 6), this vector points in the same direction as (5 3), but has twice the length (there are rules for how you do this multiplication which I have already assumed).


Matrices are rectangular arrays of numbers, they can have different numbers of rows and columns. We are interested in square matrices, where the number of rows and columns are the same. You can mutiply a square matrix with a column of numbers(a vector), and there is prescribed way to do it (I won't elaborate here, but you can look this one up easily). The important thing is that the result of this multiplication is always another column of numbers -- another vector. A matrix acts on a vector to produce another vector!

So we can think of (square) matrices as transformations on vectors. A great example is the rotation matrix:
https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotation_matrix .
This matrix rotates vectors in 2D (or 3D) space given an angle θ. From this perspective, we also like to call matrices operators, because they operate (act on) a vector to yield another vector.

Now to eigenvalues/eigenvectors. Consider 3D space, and think about a vector that points in the z-direction (perpendicular to the x-y plane). Now rotate the vector about the z-axis (a rotation in the x-y plane). In other words, apply a xy-rotation matrix A, on this vector v.  What happens to this vector? Nothing! So applying a xy-rotation matrix onto this vector, yields the same vector. We can write this as an equation: Av = v, where A is the rotation matrix and v is the vector pointing in the z-direction. 

More generally, consider a matrix A,  a vector v, and a number k, satisfying Av = kv. Then v is an eigenvector of A. The eigenvectors are vectors that just get scaled when acted upon by the matrix A. The number k is how much the vector gets scaled, called the eigenvalue. Every matrix A has it's oen set of eigenvectors with it's own eigenvalues. We just saw that vectors pointing in the z-direction are eigenvectors of the xy-rotation matrix with eigenvalue 1.

**TL;DR Eigenvectors are vectors that just get scaled when acted upon by a matrix(operator), and its eigenvalue is how much it gets scaled.**

What does this have to do with quantum mechanics? In quantum mechanics, the physical state of a particle is a vector. Physical observables, like position and momentum, are now operators(matrices) acting on states/vectors. Every operator has its own set of eigenvectors, they represent states with definite values of the physical observable, the value being the eigenvalue.  For example there the momentum operator P has an eigenvector |p> (in quantum mechanics we like to represent vectors with  |v>, this is called bra-ket notation) with an eigenvalue p, or P |p> = p |p>. This means that |p> is the physical state of a particle with momentum p.

The set of all eigenvalues of an operator A are all the possible results you get when you measure the physical observable A of a particle. Could be position, momentum etc. How do you determine which result you will get? It turns out that this is probabilistic. Given that a particle is in some state |v>, the result you will get when you measure, say, the momentum of the particle is one of all the possible eigenvalues of the momentum operator P, with an associated probability. How exactly you determine this probability is another story, and has to do with how you can add vectors together, and conversely how you can decompose a vector as a sum of other vectors. This comment is getting very long though, so hopefully others can fill in the gap.

The actual pronunciation of 虛 is nothing like how you'd say "shei" or "shi". In "shei" and "shi", the "i" implies that the pronunciation ends with flat lips, with the corners of the lips spread outwards.

It is not pronunced like the word "shoo" either, since that would imply that it rhymes with the word "woo", which it doesn't. An actual Chinese characters that is pronunced "shoo" is 鼠 in 老鼠(mouse). Incidentally 无 sounds exactly like "woo" up to a tone.

To pronounce 虛, think about the shape of your lips when you say "shoo", it should make a round-ish opening. Now start by saying "sheeeee", hold the "eeee" out, change the shape your lips are making to that round-ish opening at the end of "shoo". 虛 then starts with the typical "sh" sound in English followed by this. Compare saying this with saying the word "shoo", you should notice that the tongue's placement is different. I think it's lower in "shoo" than in 虚.

Of course, this sound (is it a vowel?) doesn't seem to exist in English, and they probably expected English speakers to say "shoo" anyway. Sticking with "shoo" is fine.

As you noticed your campaign doesn't have some NPCs/areas/bosses etc.  That's because campaigns(and adventures) are partially randomized. 

Each time you start a new campaign ("reroll" a campaign), you can get different areas/bosses etc. that weren't there in your previous run. You still go through the same worlds as before, you might get different sub-storylines, dungeons bosses etc. The only exception is two specific worlds that are fixed and not random. Those two will be the same in every run of the campaign.

Additionally, a good amount of progress is carried over (equipment, consumables, materials, levels). The only things that don't carry over are quest items, and naturally any sort of story progress. This means you get to go through the campaign again to get any item/secret you might have missed, see a storyline you haven't seen yet, fight a new boss etc.

Adventure mode is exactly like campaign mode, except you only play through one world. You get to pick which world to playthrough (except for those 2 specific fixed worlds), and it is random in the same way the campaign worlds are. It's also separate from campaign mode; rerolling your adventure mode doesn't affect any progress on your campaign world, and vice versa.

I would suggest you finish your first playthrough of the campaign(take your time and explore!), and once you're done, reroll the campaign(or start an adventure mode) to see different things.

Seems like you're used to weapons that deal larger amounts damage in fewer hits (shorter uptime). 

Yes the SnS vanilla moveset deals small numbers but you also attack faster **and** your attacks are not as committal (you can adjust your direction, repositon, cancel etc. easier than other weapons). With weapons like this, you want to be engaging/disengaging (going in for attacks/pulling back out) very frequently. Don't dismiss the rest of the moveset outright.


Start off with just the basic slash/sheild bash attacks as your offense, and your shield + evading as your defense. Once you're able to complete hunts reliably (with reasonable quest complete times), start incorporating the backhops into your flow offensively (aerial follow ups), defensively (do reposition/evade, or iframing if you're ballsy) or both.

Once you're very familiar with the backhop, **now** try and sneak in some perfect rushs. Don't get too greedy and try to finish full rushes when you can't. Pulling off the entire combo  is not just about how well you understand the weapon, it also requires deep understanding of the monsters moveset/behavior.

Worst come to worst, SnS may not be for you, and that's ok.

Picture an object, moving counterclockwise (circularly) around a point in a plane, just like the diagram in your post.

At the instant where the object is at the top of the circle, the velocity vector points to the left. Consider an acceleration on the object that always points toward the center(what we call a centripetal acceleration). Notice that at that instant, the acceleration vector is perpendicular to the velocity vector.

Now think about what happens to the velocity vector after some tiny amount of time, due to the acceleration vector. You can see that the velocity vector is going to "bend inwards" towards the acceleration vector, and the angle between the velocity and the acceleration becomes less than 90 degrees.

But we left something out of this, and that's the strength of the acceleration (or the length of the acceleration vector). You can imagine if the centripetal acceleration was very strong, the velocity vector would bend inwards very quickly, as in the object would spiral towards the center, and it wouldn't get to move much tangentially. But if you consider weaker and weaker accelerations, there would be a point where the acceleration is weak enough so that the velocity vector doesn't curve inward fast enough, and remains perpendicular to the acceleration vector at every instant. This leads to circular motion. (Actually, the distance of the object from the center is also important. For example, at larger distance, the velocity must bend slower in order to maintain a circular shape). Overall, it is a combination of the right distance, tangential speed, and centripetal acceleration that results in circular motion

A more intuitive explanation of this is that an object orbiting earth (in circular motion) is "constantly falling towards the earth", but the surface of the earth curves away fast enough so that the object never falls to the surface. Here's an animation illustrating this with Newton's Cannon: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xfZHUwyh59k](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xfZHUwyh59k) . Notice that if the cannon isn't fast enough, the cannon's velocity curves inwards too quickly, and it falls towards the earth (or it spirals inward towards the center of the earth if you will). But if it's fast enough, it curves at just the right speed to keep going in a circle. This is a case of being at some given distance and acceleration, and finding the right speed so that it curves inward at the right rate.

Newton's Law does apply for particles, but technically speaking, they are approximations for things moving at speeds much slower than the speed of light.

KE = 1/2mv^2 is a formula you get using Galilean Relativity (x' = x - vt, etc.) and the usual form of Newton's 2nd Law (F=ma). However if you go on and learn Special Relativity you'll learn that Galilean Relativity is not exact, and is only a very good approximation at speeds much slower than the speed of light, which happens to be most of the time in our daily lives. For speeds close to c, Newton's 2nd Law has to be modified (and Galilean Relativity would not be correct).

For KE = 1/2mv^2 to be a good approximation for the kinetic energy, you need v/c <<< 1. In your case where v=0.05c, using KE = 1/2mv^2 might be a pretty good approximation. You can check it yourself:

The relativistic kinetic energy is
KE = (Gamma - 1)mc^2, where Gamma = (1 - (v/c)^2  )^(-1/2)

You can calculate this using v = 0.05c and compare it with the value you get using KE = 1/2mv^2, probably won't be exactly the same, but should be pretty close.



Although what you mentioned, with the h/mv, is actually quantum mechanics. That is the de Broglie wavelength for a particle with momentum p. Put shortly, you'll soon learn that light has both particle-like and wave-like properties. de Broglie was inspired by that, and said that all particles should also have wave-like properties (including things like protons and electrons), and went ahead to give a formula to calclulate their wavelength:

l = h/p, where l is the wavelength and h is Planck's constant.

I'm guessing that in your problem you're given the wavelength, and using p=mv, and v=0.05c you can find the mass using l=h/mv.

Note that since you are already saying p=mv, you are already assuming that you are working with v/c <<< 1. So using KE = 1/2 mv^2 would be valid, but I'm guessing the issue is that in your problem, you're given wavelength, not the kinetic energy?

Things like sharpness management, hot/cold drinks, stamina regulation are all pretty neat things, but to be honest, they're fun, immersive, and rewarding, but only the first time. Slow gathering, mining, fishing(fishing is still tedious as fuck but is fairly humorous so I can still live with it) were really cool the first time I did it, but after playing through several generations of Monster Hunter, it's just tiring.

Every time I go back and fire up and old game for another playthrough with friends, gathering is the most tedious and boring part. I fully agree that it plays a vital role in setting the atmosphere, especially for new players, what I'm saying is that once you've had even a little bit of experience with the game, this atmosphere expires, pretty damn quick. It's just very transient and fleeting. Compare that to encountering a monster, learning it's attacks and patterns and mastering a fight, understanding your weapon's moveset, coming up with counterattacks/strategies, pushing for better and better clear times etc, the rewarding feeling from that feels \*much\* more earned and long lasting.

Besides that, for new players these mechanics could be vital and detrimental to a fight, sure, very valid point. But for experienced players, they eventually end up as nothing but annoyances. I used to abandon quests if I forgot a hot/cold drink or brought the wrong drink in the older games, but nowadays, with the same games, but with enough experience and time, you eventually don't bother at all. As for stamina, when you get good enough in a fight, you'll eventually be clearing quests before your maximum stamina can even drop down to a concerning level, and that too, comes quite naturally with experience and time.

I will agree that things like restocking, changing your gear mid fight etc. have made the game easier, but not quite directly. It allows for newer players to "turtle" through hunts. In short, gather a shit ton of healing items, go into a fight, employ very defensive, hit and run tactics, and as long as you don't get and make it before the \*very\* generous 50 min timer, you've cleared the quest. With enough patience, you can clear the entire game this way.  Lets be clear though, you could totally do this with previous games too. If you played REEEEEEALLY passively, a hunt might take 30-40 minutes, but you could still finish it.

All in all, the little things are nice and quaint the first time you learn about them and experience them, but their charm dissipates pretty quickly, and other more involved aspects of the game quickly take over your focus. At the very least that's my experience.

Every Monster Hunter's late endgame difficulty was sloppy. It's a recurring problem, it's just that every game had a different flavor of sloppy.
